clue.text: Newspaper publisher tries to initially

parts.note: a judge hears or tries a case in court

indicators.note: initially points at the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: first letter of to

explanation.surface: A press baron makes an effort to do something at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tries' looks like attempts, but here it is the courtroom sense.
explanation.definitionFit: William Randolph Hearst was the American press magnate who built a huge chain of newspapers.

clue.text: Murder in dwelling — bring in one branch to investigate?

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside, so these letters go into the dwelling word

parts.note: a home is a dwelling
I is the Roman numeral one
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of British police

explanation.surface: A killing inside a house calls in detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: The CID is the plain-clothes detective branch of UK police forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Homicide is the killing of one person by another, so it is a synonym for murder.

clue.text: Holding dog with no lead?

indicators.note: having no lead means the front is missing, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a basset is a short-legged hound

explanation.surface: Someone holds a dog that has slipped its lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' reads as a dog's leash, but here it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is something owned, such as a financial holding.

clue.text: Son running off, running quickly

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
running off copies on a press is printing them

explanation.surface: A boy runs away at top speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running off' looks like escaping, but it is the printing sense of running off copies.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprinting means running at full speed over a short distance.

clue.text: Deputy at university is behaving badly

parts.note: an acting head is a deputy standing in
a student who is up is in residence at university

explanation.surface: A deputy head at a university is misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' at Oxford or Cambridge is the British idiom for attending university.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is the idiom for misbehaving, as a child or a faulty machine does.

clue.text: Joiner — one living in 14?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a craftsman who makes fine wooden furniture
second meaning: the Prime Minister, resident at 14, who picks the ministers of government

explanation.walkthrough: 14 is DOWNING STREET; the Prime Minister living there forms the Cabinet, so is its maker, while a joiner makes cabinets of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A joiner is a carpenter of fine furniture, and the Prime Minister appoints the senior ministers who form the government's top committee.

clue.text: Sarah's son uses savings scheme account

parts.note: an ISA is an Individual Savings Account, a UK tax-free savings scheme
AC is the abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: Sarah's boy opens a savings account.
explanation.walkthrough: An ISA is a British tax-free savings account.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, Isaac was the son born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age.

clue.text: Got upset about reportedly lame male cat

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the sound-alike
upset means knocked over and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: reportedly means as people say it, so we want a word that sounds like a synonym

parts.note: to lame someone is to injure them; said loosely it sounds like this spelling
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A tomcat with a limp got cross.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled letters with male wrap round a sound-alike for injure; the homophone is loose, so the parse is a best reading of a rough clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A ginger tom is an orange-coated male cat, so cat defines it as a broader term.

clue.text: Boat heading for Plymouth, badly loaded, docked

indicators.note: the heading is the top, so take the first letter of the place named

parts.note: first letter of Plymouth

indicators.note: done badly means messed up, so the remaining letters are scrambled
a docked tail is cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A poorly loaded boat sails for Plymouth and ties up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Docked' suggests a moored boat; it means cut short, as a dog's tail is docked.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedalo is a small pleasure boat driven by pedals, common at British seaside resorts.

clue.text: Millions close to boundary cross Indian city

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for millions

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter, so take the end of the following word

parts.note: last letter of boundary
sore means annoyed or cross

explanation.surface: Millions near a border crossing into an Indian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a verb about crossing the boundary; it is the adjective meaning angry.
explanation.definitionFit: Mysore, now Mysuru, is a historic city in the southern Indian state of Karnataka.

clue.text: Got on a bidet, nervously

indicators.note: doing something nervously means jittery and unsettled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone climbs onto a bidet with some trepidation.
explanation.walkthrough: The comic image of a jittery bathroom user hides that 'Got' is the definition at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain something is to acquire or get it, so the past tense matches got.

clue.text: Film city in Colorado, Boulder?

parts.note: Brighton is a city near Denver in Colorado
a boulder is a large rock

explanation.surface: A film set in a Colorado city, namely Boulder.
explanation.walkthrough: Boulder looks like the Colorado city, but it is a big stone; the city is a lesser-known Colorado namesake of the English seaside town.
explanation.definitionFit: Brighton Rock is the 1947 British gangster film adapted from Graham Greene's novel.

clue.text: A batsman may to get away quickly

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a cricketer may play a cut shot and then run between the wickets
second meaning: to flee in a hurry

explanation.surface: What a cricketer might do in order to make a quick escape.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the cut is a shot played square of the wicket on the off side, after which the batsman can run.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to abandon a situation and escape swiftly, while literally describing two batting actions.

clue.text: Caught fish on river — put them in this

indicators.note: in an across answer, one thing on another is placed after it, so the fish goes behind the river

parts.note: C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
R is the abbreviation for river
an eel is a fish, placed on (after) the river letter

explanation.surface: An angler who has landed fish by a river is told where to keep them.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the surface: 'them' is the caught fish, and the answer is what an angler stores them in.
explanation.definitionFit: A creel is a wicker basket an angler carries to hold the catch.

clue.text: The way in which Eden served?

definitions.text: The way in which Eden served?

parts.words: The way in which Eden served?
parts.note: surface reading: the manner in which someone called Eden carried out duties, perhaps in a garden

parts.words: The way in which Eden served?
parts.note: setter's reading: way means a road, and Anthony Eden served as Prime Minister from the London street where the PM lives

explanation.surface: A question about how Eden performed in office, or how the garden of Eden was tended.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was the British Prime Minister in 1955-57; 'way' reads as manner but means a street.
explanation.definitionFit: Number 10 on this Westminster street is the official residence of the British Prime Minister.

clue.text: Cried after snakes exposed

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the word for cried is placed second, behind the snaking word

parts.note: a road that snakes winds
to cry is to weep

explanation.surface: Someone cried after being shown snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snakes' reads as reptiles but is the verb for twisting.
explanation.definitionFit: A windswept place is open and exposed to strong winds.

clue.text: Sword found in former burial ground around start of century

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, joined in with the rest

parts.note: ex means former

indicators.note: ground means crushed into pieces, so the word before it is broken up

parts.note: taken as written
first letter of century

explanation.surface: A legendary sword is discovered in an old burial site dating to around the turn of a century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burial ground' reads as a cemetery, but ground is the mixing signal; the century's opening letter goes in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Excalibur is King Arthur's legendary blade from Arthurian romance.

clue.text: Overwhelm one sister on tryst

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a nun is a religious sister
a tryst is a romantic date

explanation.surface: A nun on a secret romantic meeting is overcome.
explanation.definitionFit: To inundate is to flood, hence to overwhelm with a great quantity.

clue.text: Inferior batsman's guard

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in cricket, a lower-order batsman sent in late in the day to protect the better players
second meaning: a person who keeps watch over premises after dark

explanation.surface: The protective equipment belonging to a weak batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as possessive, suggesting a batsman's pads or box, but it stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a security man on duty overnight and a cricket tactic of sending in a lesser batter to shield stronger ones.

clue.text: Doctor on barge in capital city

parts.note: MO is a medical officer
a scow is a flat-bottomed barge

explanation.surface: A medic travels on a barge through a capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is often an anagram signal; here it is just a medical officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Moscow is the capital city of Russia.

clue.text: Famous group in watering hole

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Manchester rock band led by the Gallagher brothers
second meaning: a fertile spot with water in a desert

explanation.surface: A celebrity band spotted drinking in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watering hole' is slang for a pub, which suits the band, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to a famous 1990s Britpop band and also to a desert spring where animals and travellers drink.

clue.text: One entering name of musical instrument

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so this letter goes into the next word

parts.note: a big name is a star
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone enters the name of an instrument on a form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Name' as in a famous name, a celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitar is a long-necked plucked string instrument from India.

clue.text: Require, on stage, a French firearm

parts.note: to require is to need
a leg is one stage of a journey or race
un is French for a

explanation.surface: An actor needs a French gun as a prop on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On stage' suggests theatre, but stage is a leg of a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: The needle gun was a nineteenth-century Prussian breech-loading rifle fired by a long needle-like pin.

clue.text: Turned up to search a lake

definitions.text: Turned up to search a lake

indicators.note: in a down clue turned up means read from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
police drag a lake when searching it with nets or hooks

explanation.surface: Police arrived to drag a lake for a body.
explanation.walkthrough: The Garda are the Irish police: they are who turn up to drag a lake, so the whole clue is the definition; the wordplay reverses the article and the search verb, read loosely.
explanation.definitionFit: Garda is the Irish police force, the people who would arrive to search waters in an investigation.

clue.text: Play about leaving for work

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so those letters drop out of the longer word

parts.note: recreation is leisure play
re is Latin-derived for about or concerning

explanation.surface: A play about someone quitting to take a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' suggests a drama, but it means leisure; removing the opening two letters leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A creation is a work produced by an artist or maker, as in a work of art.

clue.text: I ordered a Brie in part of Europe

indicators.note: ordered means arranged, so these letters are put into a different sequence

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner orders a French cheese while on holiday somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' reads as asking for food in a restaurant, but it means rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Iberia is the peninsula in south-west Europe shared by Spain and Portugal.

clue.text: Take part in a sport and risk a wet undoing?

indicators.note: undoing something takes it apart, so the letters are pulled apart and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone joins in a sport even though a soaking may be their downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the right sport: a fall on the lake is the wet undoing.
explanation.definitionFit: To water-ski is to glide on skis behind a motorboat, a verb meaning to do that sport.

clue.text: Civilised ancient city, source of evil

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia
a bane is a cause of misery or harm

explanation.surface: An ancient city was refined yet also the root of wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur is the crossword's favourite ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Urbane describes polished, courteous and sophisticated manners, which is to say civilised.
